claimed: /menu returns HTTP 404 — the menu page is broken
actual: The menu works fine in a browser. The site builder uses client-side routing, so a direct path request 404s at the server while the in-app nav renders normally.
reason: The crawler is not a browser. It does not run JS and cannot follow client-side routes, so it reported a real HTTP status that is not what a customer experiences.
proposedRule: A bare HTTP status code from a site builder usually means client-side routing the crawler could not follow. A rendered 404 page with its own copy means the route is genuinely missing. Only the second is safe to lead with.

claimed: Site returns 'Too many redirects' — confirmed on five attempts across two days
actual: Site loads normally in a browser. The real gap is that there is no menu on the site at all; the only route in is the Order Online button.
reason: Repeated identical machine readings felt like confirmation but were the same blind spot repeated. Re-fetching does not validate a fetch-based claim.
proposedRule: When a gap claim fails verification, look for the real gap before discarding the lead — the opener is wrong, not necessarily the lead. Also: a design opinion ('menu and photos on separate screens') is not a defect and makes a weak opener.

claimed: Wix placeholder content, San Francisco demo address, no menu — a neglected site
actual: The page reading was accurate and is unchanged. But this is a site MID-BUILD, not a neglected one — the Mammoth Poke team is likely building it right now.
reason: An unfinished site and a neglected site look identical from outside and mean opposite things commercially. The observation was right; the inference was wrong.
proposedRule: Before leading with a placeholder or template-default gap, check whether the business recently opened, changed hands, or has a builder attached. If it opened in the last ~60 days, assume mid-build unless proven otherwise.

claimed: v1 drafts listed every defect found and did not say how the sender came to be looking at the page
actual: Rewritten to five beats: route disclosed, one customer-visible wall, mechanical consequence, who you are, permission-style ask.
reason: Disclosing no route and listing multiple defects reads as surveillance — like a compiled report rather than something a person happened to hit. Also: lead with the most CUSTOMER-VISIBLE defect, not the most damning one.
proposedRule: Five-beat structure, one defect only, blame the gap and never the owner, rotate beat 4 phrasing across a batch so owners comparing notes don't see identical paragraphs.

claimed: IG status marked 'active (est.)' based on a search-indexed post
actual: For two leads the only indexed post was 1-5 years old despite the businesses clearly being active.
reason: Search-indexed Instagram posts skew old even for accounts that post weekly, so an old indexed post is evidence of nothing either way.
proposedRule: When the only evidence of IG activity is an indexed post more than a year old, status is 'unconfirmed', not 'active-est'.

claimed: Hi! Went looking for your new place after hearing you'd moved to Hubbard St, and your site sent me to the old Wentworth address in Chinatown. It's the only address on there, so I figured you'd want to know. Anyone who Googles you and drives to Chinatown probably doesn't try a second time. I'm a web guy here in Chicago, I build small sites for restaurants plus a little game regulars play to win a free dish, which quietly builds you a list of people to bring back in. Happy to put together a fixed version you can look at, want me to?
actual: 您好！我周日去吃了你們的土匪烤魚，味道真的非常棒、我很喜歡！不過我也注意到當時晚餐時段的客人稍微有點稀少。另外想順便提醒您一下：我原本想找你們的新店，但貴店網站上的地址依然寫著中國城的舊址（Wentworth Ave），沒有更新到 Hubbard St。如果顧客照著網站地址跑去中國城，發現白跑一趟，恐怕就不會再試第二次了，這對晚餐生意影響蠻大的。我是芝加哥當地的網站設計師，專門幫餐廳做網站與顧客回流小互動。如果您需要的話，我很樂意免費幫您把網站上的舊地址修正過來。另外，針對晚餐時段客流的部分，我也幫其他餐廳做過一些簡單的掃碼互動小遊戲，能幫店家收集熟客名單並吸引他們回訪。如果方便的話，我做個簡單的修改預覽發給您參考看看，您看可以嗎？
reason: Rewrote in Mandarin — the owner is Chinese-speaking and a DM in their own language lands very differently. Also led with having actually eaten there and named the dish, and mentioned the quiet dinner service I saw, before raising the address problem.
proposedRule: Write the DM in the owner's own language when you can identify it. A Mandarin-speaking owner reading a Mandarin DM is a different conversation from the same message in English.

claimed: Live site is an unedited Wix demo template, verified on two fetches: footer reads "(c) 2035 by My Site", address shown is Wix's demo "500 Terry Francine Street, 6th Floor, San Francisco, CA 94158", contact is info@mysite.com / 123-456-7890, and the social buttons link to facebook.com/wix and instagram.com/wix. No menu anywhere on the site.
actual: The website is a placeholder but no address is listed
reason: Gap is real but the specifics claimed were off, or a more customer-visible defect exists.
proposedRule: Verify each specific detail in a placeholder claim, not just that the page is a placeholder. "It shows a San Francisco demo address" is a separate factual claim from "it is an unedited template" and can be false on its own.

actual: Hi! Saw the old Wave Sushi space was open again and looked you up, but noticed your site is still showing the default Wix template. Right now, anyone who lands there before finding your Toast link probably assumes you're not open yet, which means lost orders! I'm a local Chicago web designer. I build sites tailored to match a restaurant's specific decor and vibe, plus simple interactive games for regulars to win a free dish — which quietly builds a customer list you actually own. I'd be happy to mock up a quick concept of what your site could look like matching your space. Mind if I send it over?
reason: Made the cost explicit ("which means lost orders") instead of leaving it implied, and said what I actually do — sites matched to their decor and vibe — rather than just "I build websites". Ended on "Mind if I send it over?" which feels less pushy than "want to see it".
proposedRule: State the commercial cost explicitly rather than implying it. "Which means lost orders" beats leaving the owner to infer why a broken page matters.

claimed: Hi! Read the Axios piece on your lagman and went to look up your menu, which is how I ended up here. Couldn't really read it though, it's all photos, so none of the dish names are text anywhere. Means when someone searches for lagman in Chicago, yours can't come up. I'm a web guy here in Chicago, I build small sites for restaurants plus a little game regulars play to win a free dish, which quietly builds you a list of people to bring back in. Happy to put together a version you can look at if you want.
actual: Hi! Saw the Axios piece on your lagman and went straight to look up your menu, but noticed it's currently uploaded as image files rather than text. The big issue there is searchability — Google can't read the text inside image files, so when people in Chicago search for "best lagman," your site isn't showing up to those potential customers! I'm a web designer here in Chicago. I build clean, mobile-friendly sites for local restaurants, plus simple interactive games for regulars to win a free dish — which quietly builds a customer list you actually own to bring people back in. I'd be happy to mock up a searchable version of your menu so you can see what it looks like. Mind if I send it over?
reason: Named the mechanism plainly — Google cannot read text inside images — rather than assuming the owner already knows why an image menu hurts. Owners do not think in SEO terms; spelling out the cause makes the problem feel real.
proposedRule: Name the mechanism behind the problem. Owners do not think in SEO terms — "Google cannot read text inside an image" makes an image menu feel real in a way that "it is not searchable" does not.
